claims.text: Low-dimensional FeMnNiGeSi films and nanoribbons have a reduced magnetocaloric response and persistent hysteresis under low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Defect- and interface-induced inhomogeneity governs the reduced magnetocaloric response and hysteresis by pinning magnetic domain walls.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi microstructure contains significant residual strain, small grains, and disordered interfaces.
Residual strain, small grains, and disordered interfaces inhibit a sharp magnetostructural transition.
Defect relaxation and reduced interfacial strain can partially restore cooperative magnetic ordering.
Partially restored cooperative magnetic ordering will enhance the magnetocaloric effect and narrow magnetic hysteresis.
Controlled post-deposition laser or rapid thermal annealing will relieve residual interfacial strain.
Controlled post-deposition annealing will promote moderate grain coarsening without causing full crystallographic ordering or significant compositional segregation.
Defect-rich grain boundaries and strained interfaces act as magnetic-domain-wall pinning centers.
Localized strain fields from defects and nanostructured interfaces disrupt uniform magnetic ordering.
Defects and nanostructured interfaces slow magnetic-domain reorientation.
Slower domain reorientation hampers the sharp magnetocaloric transition and increases hysteresis.
Annealing-induced defect and strain reduction will permit more coherent magnetic-domain motion and stronger coupling between magnetic and thermal responses.
Annealed samples will exhibit a larger isothermal entropy change or adiabatic temperature change than the as-deposited baseline during low-field cycling.
Annealed samples will exhibit narrower magnetization hysteresis loops and lower energy loss per cycle than the as-deposited baseline.
Poor heat transfer in the low-dimensional as-deposited state contributes to the diminished response and larger hysteresis.
The proposed mechanism applies at magnetic fields below approximately 100–200 mT and at cycle periods of approximately seconds, long enough to reach thermal equilibrium.
An inert annealing atmosphere is needed to prevent oxidation.
The proposed mechanism operates for film thicknesses or nanoribbon widths from tens to a few hundred nanometers.
Excessive grain growth or secondary-phase formation could degrade magnetocaloric performance.
